variants.title: Choose the record key
variants.context: Kafka’s core invariant is ordered, append-only history within one partition. A record key chooses the partition, so key design chooses the scope of ordering, parallelism, and hotspot risk. There is no global order across a topic.
variants.prompt: Events for one order must be consumed in the order they happened. Which key?
options: order_id.
A random UUID per record.
No key.
optionFeedback: Same key, same partition, so per-order order is preserved.
Random keys spread writes but discard per-entity order.
Unkeyed records are distributed without ordering.
variants.explanation: Choose the smallest business identity whose events must stay ordered.

variants.title: Choose the record key
variants.context: Kafka’s core invariant is ordered, append-only history within one partition. A record key chooses the partition, so key design chooses the scope of ordering, parallelism, and hotspot risk. There is no global order across a topic.
variants.prompt: A team keys everything by tenant_id, and one tenant produces 60% of traffic. What happens?
options: That tenant’s partition becomes a hotspot while others idle.
Kafka spreads the hot key across partitions automatically.
Nothing; partitions are elastic.
optionFeedback: One dominant key preserves order while concentrating traffic on one partition.
A key maps to one partition.
Partitions have a per-partition load envelope.
variants.hint: What does a single dominant key do to one partition?
variants.explanation: Measure the largest key’s share and decide how to isolate or subdivide that entity.

variants.title: Choose the record key
variants.context: Kafka’s core invariant is ordered, append-only history within one partition. A record key chooses the partition, so key design chooses the scope of ordering, parallelism, and hotspot risk. There is no global order across a topic.
variants.prompt: Consumers rely on records from different orders arriving in a particular relative order. Is that safe?
options: No. Kafka orders within a partition only; there is no global order across a topic.
Yes, if the producer sends them in order.
Yes, with a single consumer.
optionFeedback: Different keys may land on different partitions.
Producer send order does not survive across partitions.
One consumer still reads several partitions independently.
variants.hint: What is the scope of ordering?
variants.explanation: Do not rely on accidental ordering between unrelated keys; a partition-count change would break it.

variants.title: Compose durability
variants.context: Replication factor is how many copies exist. acks decides what completes a send: acks=0 no confirmation, acks=1 leader append only, acks=all the required in-sync replicas. min.insync.replicas can reject a write when too few replicas are caught up.
variants.prompt: With acks=1, the leader acknowledges and then fails before followers copy the record. What happened?
options: The acknowledged write can be lost.
The write is safe on the followers.
Kafka rejects the write.
optionFeedback: Leader-only confirmation covers a single copy.
Followers had not copied it yet.
acks=1 does not reject on missing replicas.
variants.hint: How many copies existed at acknowledgement time?
variants.explanation: Pair acks=all with a meaningful min.insync.replicas for writes that must survive a broker loss.

variants.title: Compose durability
variants.context: Replication factor is how many copies exist. acks decides what completes a send: acks=0 no confirmation, acks=1 leader append only, acks=all the required in-sync replicas. min.insync.replicas can reject a write when too few replicas are caught up.
variants.prompt: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 and only one in-sync replica available. What does the producer see?
options: The write is rejected; a possible durability loss becomes visible unavailability.
The write succeeds on the leader.
The write waits forever.
optionFeedback: That trade is the point of min.insync.replicas.
acks=all requires the configured in-sync count.
Rejection is immediate and explicit.
variants.hint: Would you rather lose data silently or fail loudly?
variants.explanation: min.insync.replicas converts a silent durability gap into an explicit error.

variants.title: Compose durability
variants.context: Replication factor is how many copies exist. acks decides what completes a send: acks=0 no confirmation, acks=1 leader append only, acks=all the required in-sync replicas. min.insync.replicas can reject a write when too few replicas are caught up.
variants.prompt: Producer idempotence is enabled. Does a database write triggered by the consumer now happen exactly once?
options: No. Idempotence deduplicates broker retries within the producer protocol only.
Yes.
Yes, if acks=all.
optionFeedback: It does not deduplicate a new application send, nor an external side effect.
The guarantee stops at the Kafka boundary.
acks affects durability, not external effects.
variants.hint: Where does the producer’s guarantee end?
variants.explanation: Use an idempotency key, inbox/outbox, or reconciliation at the external boundary.

variants.title: Size the topic
variants.context: Retained replica bytes = logical ingress × retention seconds × replication factor. Active consumers = the smaller of consumer instances and partition count. Per-consumer demand = events per second ÷ active consumers.
variants.prompt: Logical ingress is 5 MB per second, retention is 10 hours, and replication factor is 3. How many GB are retained across replicas?

mistakes.feedback: That forgets the replication factor of three.

variants.title: Size the topic
variants.context: Retained replica bytes = logical ingress × retention seconds × replication factor. Active consumers = the smaller of consumer instances and partition count. Per-consumer demand = events per second ÷ active consumers.
variants.prompt: A topic has 12 partitions and the consumer group runs 20 instances. How many instances actively consume?
variants.hint: Each partition goes to at most one group member at a time.
variants.explanation: Active consumers = min(20, 12) = 12. Eight instances sit idle.

mistakes.feedback: A partition cannot be shared by two members of one group.

variants.title: Size the topic
variants.context: Retained replica bytes = logical ingress × retention seconds × replication factor. Active consumers = the smaller of consumer instances and partition count. Per-consumer demand = events per second ÷ active consumers.
variants.prompt: 6,000 events per second flow to 12 active consumers. What is the per-consumer demand?
variants.explanation: 6,000 ÷ 12 = 500 events per second each, assuming even keys.

mistakes.feedback: Divide by the 12 active consumers, not 20 instances.
The load is shared across consumers.

variants.title: Plan the partitions
variants.context: Partition by the ordering boundary: name the ordered entity, estimate the hottest key, budget partition load, and preserve routing evolution. Changing partition count later changes key-to-partition mapping for future records.
variants.prompt: A team plans partitions for order events. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Estimate the hottest key’s share of traffic.
Budget partition load from benchmarked size, compression, and acks.
Version partitioning rules and treat a partition-count change as an ordering review.

variants.hint: The invariant comes first; capacity comes after.
variants.explanation: Invariant → skew → capacity → evolution. Partition count is both a capacity decision and an API contract.

variants.title: Plan the partitions
variants.context: Partition by the ordering boundary: name the ordered entity, estimate the hottest key, budget partition load, and preserve routing evolution. Changing partition count later changes key-to-partition mapping for future records.
variants.prompt: Device telemetry needs per-device order. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Choose device_id as the ordered identity.
Find the noisiest devices and plan isolation.
Divide peak load by a conservative per-partition envelope.
Keep routing rules versioned for later changes.

variants.explanation: Measure the largest key before dividing load by partition envelope.

variants.title: Plan the partitions
variants.context: Partition by the ordering boundary: name the ordered entity, estimate the hottest key, budget partition load, and preserve routing evolution. Changing partition count later changes key-to-partition mapping for future records.
variants.prompt: Partition count must grow. Put the review in order.

items.text: Confirm which entity’s ordering the topic promises.
Re-check hot keys under the new mapping.
Treat the change as an ordering and replay review, not a scaling toggle.

variants.hint: Increasing partitions changes key-to-partition mapping for future records.
variants.explanation: Consumers must not rely on accidental cross-key ordering, or a partition change breaks them.

variants.title: Read the offset
variants.context: Committed offsets are consumer progress, not proof that an external side effect happened once. Kafka transactions cover consume, produce, and offset commit inside Kafka; they do not include an external database or API.
variants.prompt: A consumer commits offset 500. Does that prove the side effect for record 499 happened exactly once?
options: No. Committed offsets are progress, not proof of an external effect.
Yes.
Yes, if the commit was synchronous.
optionFeedback: A crash between effect and commit, or between commit and effect, breaks the link.
Offsets describe reading position.
Commit mode does not include external systems.
variants.hint: What does an offset actually record?
variants.explanation: Make consumer progress match completed work with idempotent effects.

variants.title: Read the offset
variants.context: Committed offsets are consumer progress, not proof that an external side effect happened once. Kafka transactions cover consume, produce, and offset commit inside Kafka; they do not include an external database or API.
variants.prompt: A Kafka transaction consumes, produces to Kafka, and commits offsets atomically. Does it include the payment API call?
options: No. Transactions cover Kafka participants only.
Yes.
Yes, when consumers read committed data.
optionFeedback: Use an idempotency key or outbox at the external boundary.
External APIs are outside the transaction.
Read-committed affects visibility, not external calls.
variants.explanation: Kafka transactions are Kafka-only; the external boundary still needs its own contract.

variants.title: Read the offset
variants.context: Committed offsets are consumer progress, not proof that an external side effect happened once. Kafka transactions cover consume, produce, and offset commit inside Kafka; they do not include an external database or API.
variants.prompt: Consumer lag is growing while throughput looks fine. What does lag measure?
options: The distance between the latest offset and the committed offset.
Broker disk usage.
The number of partitions.
optionFeedback: Lag is how far behind committed progress is.
Disk is a different signal.
Partition count is fixed configuration.
variants.hint: Which two positions does lag compare?
variants.explanation: Slow handlers create lag, missed poll deadlines, and repeated work after rebalances.
